newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Fund managers at ease over Hong Kong handover.
newsitem.headline: Fund managers at ease over Hong Kong handover.

text.p: Whatever worries equity funds have over the risks of investing in Hong Kong next year, the handover of power to China from Britain is not one of them.
Some managers of Asia's multi-billion-dollar unit trusts say they are concerned the colony's stock market may have peaked for a while and others argue its property market may be overvalued.
But almost all expect an orderly transition of power on the night of June 30, 1997.

"I am assuming the handover will go smoothly," said Kim Teo, managing director of Credit Lyonnais Asset Management. "Sure, you're not going to put 100 percent of an Asian index into Hong Kong, but I would be happy with it heavily overweighted."
Asian funds assess Hong Kong as worth slightly under a third of the region's market capitalisation excluding Japan, but give it around a 40 percent weighting.
Most of the reason for this overweighting is based on the potential for both Hong Kong and Chinese stock markets once a successful handover has been completed, they say.

"They are still below the relative value of other markets based on political concerns, but unless things really go wrong and you get Chinese troops marching through cities, that will correct," said Teo.
He sees Hong Kong worth a 40 to 45 percent weighting and thinks the market could continue to rise next year.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng index fell 2.88 percent to 13,102.73 points on Friday, ending an almost uninterrupted bull run which took the index to an intra-day high of 13,744.30 on November 28.
Some funds saw the fall as a necessary correction and warned the Hong Kong stock market was too closely identified with the property market, which might be ready for a fall.

"We are sceptics on Hong Kong," said Hugh Young, director of Abtrust Fund Managers in Singapore. "But not because we don't think the handover won't be smooth...I can't see the value there, in view of its recent rise."

He said the heavy weighting of the stock market towards property stocks, which accounted for 60 percent of companies, left it vulnerable to a correction once borders were opened and new supplies of real estate became accessible.
Abtrust has cut Hong Kong to a 16 percent weighting. Many of the components in that weighting are companies with much more regional exposure such as Hong Kong and Shanghai Banking Corp, Abtrust says.
"That is not really a Hong Kong stock," Young said.
Another Singapore-based fund manager, who declined to be identified, said some slight cutting of Hong Kong's weighting ahead of Chinese rule could occur.
He said Singapore, widely considered "safe but unexciting", would probably benefit if there was any pull-out of funds from Hong Kong before it became Chinese. But this was unlikely.
"A year ago, political risk in Hong Kong was at the top of our minds, but at this stage we are happy about it," he said.
Alfred Lo, the director of investment at ImPac Asset Management in Hong Kong, agreed.
"One cannot afford not to be in China," he told a conference in Singapore this week. "As far as I am concerned, 1997 has already happened."
